questions.question: What is the most useful first step when a patient says they are dizzy?
choices: Classify the symptom using timing, triggers, associated symptoms, and functional effect
Assume the patient has vertigo
Order brain imaging for every episode
Diagnose anxiety before checking vital signs
questions.explanation: Dizziness is nonspecific. A time- and trigger-based syndrome approach helps distinguish vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, and nonspecific lightheadedness while preserving safety.

questions.question: Which presentation most strongly raises concern for posterior-circulation stroke rather than uncomplicated BPPV?
choices: Continuous acute vertigo with new inability to walk and diplopia
Brief spinning when rolling over in bed with normal gait between episodes
Stable motion sensitivity after a long car ride
Mild lightheadedness after skipping breakfast
questions.explanation: Continuous acute vestibular symptoms with severe gait difficulty, diplopia, focal neurologic signs, or high vascular risk can be central. They require urgent stroke-capable assessment.

questions.question: Which history is most consistent with a BPPV pattern when red flags are absent?
choices: Brief recurrent spinning triggered by rolling in bed or looking up
Hours of chest pain with collapse
Persistent focal weakness
Syncope during exercise without prodrome
questions.explanation: BPPV often produces brief triggered episodes with head-position changes. Central symptoms, chest symptoms, or exertional collapse require a different safety pathway.

questions.question: What is syncope?
choices: Transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion with rapid onset and spontaneous complete recovery
Any fall in an older adult
A prolonged postictal state after seizure
A sensation of nausea without loss of consciousness
questions.explanation: Syncope is defined by transient global cerebral hypoperfusion. Witness history is useful because seizure, mechanical fall, intoxication, and syncope can be confused in real cases.

questions.question: Which feature increases concern for cardiac syncope?
choices: Syncope during exertion or while supine, palpitations, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, or family history of sudden death
A clear vasovagal prodrome after a painful blood draw
Brief dizziness when standing after dehydration
Mild nausea after eating
questions.explanation: Exertional or supine syncope, cardiac history, palpitations, abnormal ECG, and family sudden-death history are high-risk features that lower the threshold for emergency or cardiology-directed assessment.

questions.question: What role should a resting 12-lead ECG have in an initial syncope evaluation?
choices: It should be obtained as part of the initial assessment; if unavailable in the setting, that limitation informs risk-based disposition
It proves all episodes are vasovagal
It replaces history and examination
It is only needed after a normal cardiac evaluation
questions.explanation: A resting ECG is an important initial syncope tool. Its findings—and the inability to obtain one in a higher-risk setting—must be interpreted alongside history, vital signs, examination, and risk context.

questions.question: Why is medication review essential in dizziness or presyncope?
choices: Recent starts, dose changes, intermittent use, and interactions of antihypertensives, diuretics, psychoactive drugs, sedatives, and diabetes therapies can contribute
Medications cannot affect blood pressure or balance
Only antibiotics matter
It is unnecessary when orthostatic hypotension is found
questions.explanation: Medication effects can cause or worsen hypotension, hypoglycemia, sedation, and balance problems. They can coexist with more dangerous causes, so review informs but does not end evaluation.

questions.question: Which patient needs emergency evaluation rather than a routine positional maneuver?
choices: A patient with new vertigo, severe headache, slurred speech, and unilateral weakness
A patient with brief reproducible positional spinning and normal neurologic examination
A patient who wants fall-prevention tips
A patient with a stable prior BPPV diagnosis and no new symptoms
questions.explanation: New focal neurologic symptoms and severe headache are stroke red flags. Do not perform or prescribe a BPPV maneuver before the central neurologic risk is addressed.

questions.question: What is the safest interpretation of orthostatic hypotension in a patient with syncope?
choices: It can contribute to symptoms but does not automatically exclude arrhythmia, bleeding, or another serious cause
It proves the episode was harmless
It means an ECG is never needed
It eliminates the need to assess medication changes
questions.explanation: Orthostatic findings can be clinically meaningful, but the whole history and risk profile determine whether other dangerous causes still need evaluation.

questions.question: What does safe FNP disposition after a dizziness or syncope visit include?
choices: A documented syndrome and differential, urgency decision, return precautions, fall precautions when relevant, and a specific follow-up plan
Only a diagnosis code
Reassurance without checking risk
No plan if symptoms are intermittent
questions.explanation: Disposition is part of diagnostic safety. Explicit return precautions and follow-up protect the patient if the initial pattern evolves or if outpatient uncertainty remains.
